newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Worst-hit Africa gives little thought to AIDS day.
newsitem.headline: Worst-hit Africa gives little thought to AIDS day.

text.p: Africa largely ignored World AIDS Day on Sunday, many of its people caught in bloody ethnic wars that seem more pressing than a disease that has tragically become part of the continent's landscape.

Nearly 65 percent of the world's sufferers from AIDS (Aquired Immunity Deficiency Syndrome) live in Africa, believed to be the original home of the disease that has contributed to the deaths of six million people around the globe.
South Africa, Uganda and Zimbabwe were among the few African countries where the U.N.-backed AIDS awareness day was marked.
At sunset in Cape Town, anti-AIDS campaigners trained red floodlights on the rocky face of Table Mountain, a striking landmark that rises vertically from the continent's southern tip.
The colour red, usually in the form of a ribbon, has become the international symbol of the fight against the disease, often spread by sexual contact or contaminated blood.
Organisers of the Cape Town event hope to raise funds to help sufferers of the disease amid widespread criticism of the anti-AIDS efforts of President Nelson Mandela's government.
His health minister, Nkosazana Zuma, faced calls to resign for wasting money after she approved expenditure of 14 million rand ($3 million) on a single play intended to promote safe sex.
One of South Africa's four Nobel peace prize winners, Archbishop Desmond Tutu, went on television on Sunday to urge South Africans that if they could not be good, they should be careful.
"We in the church believe that sex should take place only within marriage," he said.
"However, I want to urge all those who choose to have sex outside of marriage to take the right precautions and practise safer sex. Please use a condom."
Those trying to fight AIDS in Africa report their work is hampered by ignorance and deep-seated beliefs about sex.
"A lot of our work is trying to destroy myths and misconceptions," said Andrew Hobbs, a volunteer with an anti-AIDS project in Zambia.
He said some young women there believed their vaginas would grow closed if they did not have sex, while many men feared their semen or sex organs would rot if not used.

According to some estimates, AIDS could cut life expectancy in South Africa to 40 years from 63 in less than 15 years. The deadly combination of AIDS and tuberculosis is threatening production levels in the country's labour-intensive gold mining industry.
AIDS has cut life expectancy by 10 years in Uganda, but the doctor in charge of the country's campaign against the disease expressed guarded optimism on Sunday.
"The incidence of AIDS has dropped dramatically in the 14 to 24-year-old age group -- a clear result of the campaign to increase awareness of the danger AIDS represents," said Elizabeth Madraa.
In Harare, a leading Zimbabwean group fighting the spread of AIDS petitioned the government to make the female condom freely and cheaply available.

Women and AIDS Support Network spokesman Priscilla Misihairabwi said the focus on the male condom had failed to stem the pandemic because the majority of men refused to use it, particularly with their wives.
